articles.title: Jason Heyward yacht outing with wife Vedrana offers ‘rare’ glimpse into life after Cubs retirement
articles.summary: MLB News: Former Chicago Cubs outfielder Jason Heyward is enjoying more time away from baseball after ending his 16-year MLB career earlier this year. The retir.
articles.body: Former Chicago Cubs outfielder Jason Heyward is enjoying more time away from baseball after ending his 16-year MLB career earlier this year. The retired All-Star recently shared a relaxed summer moment with his wife, Vedrana, during a yacht outing. Vedrana posted pictures from the trip on her Instagram Story, including a photo of the couple together and another showing her feet in the water. She captioned one post, “Hey babe,” and wrote, “Love you summertime chi,” on another. The outing comes as Heyward begins a new chapter with the Los Angeles Dodgers.Jason Heyward and Vedrana Heyward share a summer momentVedrana Heyward gave followers a small look at their time on the water this week. In one Instagram Story, she posed with Jason Heyward while wearing a brown bikini. Another picture showed the view from the yacht as she relaxed with her feet in the water.The posts offered a simple look at the couple's life away from the baseball field. Heyward and Vedrana have been married since March 2021 and have two children, Messi and Slaš. Their family life has mostly stayed away from the spotlight, although Vedrana has supported Heyward throughout his playing career.She has also built work of her own through Girls on the Diamond. The program was launched alongside the Jason Heyward Baseball Academy and focuses on giving young women opportunities through sports, mentorship and leadership. The program is part of the couple's wider effort to support young people in Chicago.Heyward's retirement became official in March 2026. MLB.com reported that he announced the decision on March 27 after 16 seasons in the majors. He finished his career as a five-time Gold Glove winner, an All-Star and a two-time World Series champion. His first championship came with the Cubs in 2016.Jason Heyward starts a new role with the Los Angeles DodgersRetirement did not keep Jason Heyward away from baseball for long. In May, the Los Angeles Times reported that the Dodgers brought him back as a special assistant in their front office.Heyward said he wanted to learn more about the business side of baseball. His new duties include taking part in draft meetings, meeting new players and spending time around the team's affiliates. He can also return to the clubhouse and share his experience with players and staff.The role gives Heyward a chance to learn how a team works beyond the field. He told the Los Angeles Times that he hopes to keep learning about scouting, player evaluation, research and analytics as he moves toward the next part of his career.Heyward's final playing season came with the San Diego Padres in 2025. He played 34 games before finishing his 16-year career. Before that, he spent the biggest part of his career with the Cubs from 2016 through 2022. He also played for the Atlanta Braves, St. Louis Cardinals, Dodgers and Houston Astros.For now, Heyward has both baseball and family life keeping him busy. His yacht outing with Vedrana offered a brief glimpse of the quieter side of that new chapter.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “Having someone who truly understands the discipline of sport makes all the difference” - How Shohei Ohtani and Mamiko Tanaka turned parenthood into a grounded love story
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani has achieved almost everything a baseball player could dream of.
articles.body: Shohei Ohtani has achieved almost everything a baseball player could dream of. The Los Angeles Dodgers star has a record $700 million contract, historic batting and pitching numbers, and two consecutive World Series titles. But away from the stadium, he has kept one part of his life largely private. His relationship with former Japanese basketball player Mamiko Tanaka has grown without the usual attention that follows a global sports star. From their marriage announcement in 2024 to welcoming two children, the couple have built a family life while keeping many personal details to themselves.How did Shohei Ohtani and Mamiko Tanaka meet through their sporting careers?Before becoming known as Shohei Ohtani’s wife, Mamiko Tanaka had built her own career in basketball. Born on December 11, 1996, in Tokyo, she played college basketball at Waseda University and later joined Japan’s Fujitsu Red Wave in 2019. She competed in the Women’s Japan Basketball League for four seasons before retiring in 2023.Tanaka also represented Japan at the 2017 Summer Universiade, where the team won a silver medal. At 5 feet 11 inches, she played as a forward and had experience competing at both university and professional levels. Her sporting background gave her an understanding of the time, effort and discipline needed to compete at a high level.Ohtani and Tanaka had known each other for around three to four years before he announced their marriage. However, neither has shared a detailed account of how they first met. Reports about their relationship remained limited, even as Ohtani became one of the most recognised Japanese athletes in the world.During a conversation with reporters in February 2024, Ohtani spoke about the connection they shared. He said:“She has a great understanding of my profession,” Ohtani said. “She’s willing to be wherever I want to play at. Ultimately, it was up to me. So it had nothing to do with it.”His comments offered a rare look at their relationship. Rather than discussing his personal life at length, he spoke about the understanding and support he received from his partner.Why did Shohei Ohtani surprise fans with his marriage announcement in 2024?On February 29, 2024, Ohtani shared news of his marriage through Instagram. The announcement came as a surprise because he had rarely spoken about his romantic life in public. He confirmed that he had married a Japanese woman but did not reveal her name or share many details about their relationship.Speaking to reporters during spring training, he explained why he had chosen that time to make the news public.“I felt like it was good timing because it was before the season,” Ohtani said. “I didn’t want any distractions when the season started. And I would have liked to announce it earlier, but there was some paperwork issues that lagged the whole process. So that was the whole deal.”He also said that the two had known each other for three to four years. At the time, he described his wife as a normal Japanese woman who was special to him.The identity of his wife became clearer in March 2024. As the Dodgers prepared to travel to South Korea for their season-opening series, Ohtani appeared in a photograph with Tanaka alongside other members of the team. That was the first time the public got a clear look at the woman he had married.Tanaka later appeared with him at several public events. The couple attended the Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation’s Blue Diamond Gala in May 2024, marking their red-carpet debut together. She was also seen supporting him during games and team celebrations.How did Shohei Ohtani and Mamiko Tanaka welcome their two children?Their family grew in April 2025, when Ohtani announced that Tanaka had given birth to their first child, a daughter. He shared the news on Instagram with a photograph of the baby’s feet, keeping her face and name private.Ohtani also thanked his wife for giving birth and shared how becoming a father had changed their lives.“I am so grateful to my loving wife who gave birth to our healthy beautiful daughter,” he wrote. “To my daughter, thank you for making us very nervous yet super anxious parents.”He missed a game against the Texas Rangers to be with his wife before the birth. The Dodgers placed him on the paternity list, and he returned to the lineup on April 20, 2025.The couple welcomed their second child in June 2026. Ohtani shared the news on Instagram on June 20, with a picture showing the newborn’s feet and hands. The announcement did not reveal the baby’s name or gender.In their joint message, the couple expressed their happiness and thanked those who had supported them.“We are again overjoyed to experience this wonderful day in our lives together. Thank you for being born safely. We would also like to express our heartfelt gratitude to everyone who has supported us throughout this journey.”Ohtani also missed the Dodgers’ game against the Baltimore Orioles on June 19 to be with his family. He returned to the lineup the following day and hit a home run against Baltimore.What makes Shohei Ohtani and Mamiko Tanaka’s relationship special?Ohtani and Tanaka have chosen to share only small parts of their personal lives with the public. Even after their marriage became known, they continued to keep their family away from unnecessary attention. Their decision to protect their children’s privacy has remained consistent with the way Ohtani handled his relationship before it became public.Their sporting backgrounds also give their partnership a shared point of understanding. Tanaka knows what it takes to train and compete professionally, while Ohtani continues to balance the demands of being both a pitcher and a hitter in Major League Baseball.For Ohtani, the biggest moments of his career have often happened in front of thousands of fans. His marriage and the births of his children, however, have been shared through brief personal announcements rather than lengthy public appearances. That contrast offers a glimpse of how the baseball star separates his professional success from his life at home.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Pablo Sandoval Officially Retires, Former MLB All-Star Won 3 World Series With Giants
articles.summary: MLB third baseman Pablo Sandoval, dubbed the "Kung Fu Panda" during his playing career, retired on Sunday.
articles.body:
MLB third baseman Pablo Sandoval, dubbed the "Kung Fu Panda" during his playing career, retired on Sunday.

He last played in Major League Baseball for the Atlanta Braves in the 2021 season.

Sandoval, 40, played for the San Francisco Giants (2008-14, 2017-20), Boston Red Sox (2015-17) and the Braves (2020-21). He was a three-time World Series champion and an All-Star in the 2011-12 seasons. For his career, he hit .278 with 153 homers, 639 RBI, 548 runs and a .773 OPS.

He was a postseason monster during San Francisco's 2012 and 2014 titles, hitting .364 with six homers and 13 RBI in the 2012 run and .366 with five RBI in the 2014 playoffs. He was the 2012 World Series MVP and his Game 1 performance in that series remains the stuff of legend.

He wasn't the same player after his first stint with the Giants, however, as injury issues and declining play made the five-year, $95 million contract he signed with the Red Sox ahead of the 2015 season a massive disappointment in Boston.

In San Francisco, however, he'll forever be a legend.

articles.title: Ranking Every Player on the 2027 MLB Hall of Fame Ballot
articles.summary: The 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame ballot was released by the Baseball Writers' Association of America on Monday, with Buster Posey and Jon Lester headlining the list of newcomers joining 13 holdovers from last year's ballot.
articles.body:
The 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame ballot was released by the Baseball Writers' Association of America on Monday, with Buster Posey and Jon Lester headlining the list of newcomers joining 13 holdovers from last year's ballot.

Among the returning candidates, Chase Utley (59.1 percent), Andy Pettitte (48.5 percent) and Félix Hernández (46.1 percent) came the closest to receiving the 75 percent of votes necessary for induction, and they could get another boost in a thin class of newcomers.

Posey and Lester are the biggest names among newcomers, while Jake Arrieta, Jay Bruce, Brett Gardner and Ryan Zimmerman are among the other first-time eligible players with a chance to stick around on the ballot.

Voting results for the 2027 Hall of Fame class will be revealed on Jan. 19, but for now, here is a ranking of every player on the ballot, ordered based on their career stats, peak performance, accolades, reputation and likelihood of being enshrined.

Editor's Note: Portions of this article appeared in last year's version of our Hall of Fame ballot rankings.

27. 2B/SS Starlin Castro (18.2 WAR): Made his MLB debut at 20 years old and had 1,617 hits before his age-30 season, but played just 103 games in his 30s. In 2021, MLB suspended Castro for 30 games for violating its domestic violence policy.

26. IF Asdrúbal Cabrera (30.1 WAR): Tallied 1,763 hits, 195 home runs and 869 RBI over 15 seasons, and made back-to-back AL All-Star teams in 2011 and 2012 during his time in Cleveland.

25. SP Ervin Santana (27.0 WAR): An All-Star with the Angels in 2008 and the Twins in 2017, he went 151-129 with a 4.11 ERA and 1,978 strikeouts in 2,486.2 innings, finishing in the top 10 in the AL in innings pitched four times.

24. RP Joakim Soria (18.6 WAR): Ranks 45th all-time in saves (229) and 67th in games pitched (773), and enjoyed a terrific peak with the Royals that included two 40-save seasons and a pair of All-Star selections.

23. RP Wade Davis (10.3 WAR): Davis spent two seasons in the Tampa Bay rotation before shifting to a relief role and developing into a three-time All-Star. During the Royals' pennant-winning seasons in 2014 and 2015, he posted a combined 0.97 ERA, 0.82 WHIP, 12.1 K/9 and 7.3 WAR in 140 appearances. He also led the NL in saves (43) as a member of the Rockies in 2018.

22. RP Andrew Miller (7.7 WAR): Miller was traded from Detroit to Florida in the Miguel Cabrera blockbuster early in his career, and while he flamed out as a starter, he reinvented himself as one of baseball's most dominant relievers. His 2016 postseason (10 G, 2 W, 1 SV, 5 HLD, 1.40 ERA, 30 K, 19.1 IP) was the stuff of legend and earned him ALCS MVP.

21. 3B Kyle Seager (37.0 WAR): Seager quietly spent more than a decade manning the hot corner for the Mariners, reaching 20 home runs in every full season of his career, including career-high marks in home runs (35) and RBI (101) in his final year. He tallied 242 home runs, 807 RBI and won a Gold Glove in 2014.

A three-time World Series champion and 2012 World Series MVP, Sandoval hit .338/.386/.535 with six home runs and 20 RBI in 42 career playoff games while serving as a cornerstone piece of the Giants' three titles in five years. He was also a two-time All-Star who logged a 111 OPS+ over 5,052 career plate appearances, and developed into a valuable pinch hitter later in his career.

From No. 1 prospect in baseball prior to the 2008 season to a staple in the middle of the Cincinnati lineup, Bruce had five 30-homer seasons and slugged 319 total long balls over his 14 big league seasons. A three-time All-Star and two-time Silver Slugger, he hit 233 of his home runs during his time in Cincinnati, good for eighth all-time in the long history of the organization.

A well-rounded player who provided standout defense, speed and on-base ability over a 14-year career spent entirely in Yankees pinstripes, Gardner had nine seasons with at least 3 WAR. He had 1,470 hits, 139 home runs and 274 steals while earning an All-Star selection in 2015 and winning a Gold Glove in 2016.

Widely regarded as one of the best defensive shortstops in baseball history, Vizquel won 11 Gold Glove Awards over 24 seasons and finished with a middling 82 OPS+. He also faced a civil lawsuit alleging sexual harassment; the claims were dismissed following a confidential settlement in 2022. After receiving just 18.4 percent support in 2026, he faces long odds heading into his 10th and final year on the BBWAA ballot.

Arrieta had a short peak, but during his four full seasons in the Cubs' starting rotation, he went 64-29 with a 2.67 ERA, 1.03 WHIP and 756 strikeouts in 751.1 innings. He won 2015 NL Cy Young honors, going 22-6 with a 1.77 ERA in 229 innings, and he was a key cog in the North Siders' World Series run the following year.

K-Rod burst onto the scene during the 2002 postseason, posting a 1.93 ERA with 28 strikeouts in 18.2 innings while tallying five wins and three holds as a 20-year-old rookie for the eventual World Series champion Angels. He quickly developed into one of the league's best closers in the years that followed, setting the single-season record with 62 saves in 2008 and racking up 437 career saves in 16 seasons to rank sixth on the all-time list.

"Mr. National" was the first draft pick in Nationals history following the club's move from Montreal, and he was a staple in the middle of the lineup for more than a decade. He racked up 1,846 hits, 417 doubles, 284 home runs and 1,061 RBI, and he was a two-time All-Star, two-time Silver Slugger winner and one-time Gold Glove winner across 16 seasons.

Over his first six full seasons in the majors before injuries derailed his career, Wright hit .306/.387/.515 for a 137 OPS+ while averaging 42 doubles, 27 home runs, 108 RBI, 103 runs scored, 23 steals and 5.2 WAR per 162 games. He played only 77 games after his age-31 season before spinal stenosis eventually ended his career. Otherwise, he might have been a no-doubt Hall of Famer.

With 2,452 hits, 353 home runs, 1,391 RBI and nine Gold Glove Awards, Hunter is one of the best two-way outfielders in the last 50 years. He was arguably the best defensive player in baseball at his peak with the Minnesota Twins, and he continued to produce well into his late 30s. He has yet to break 10 percent voting support in six years on the ballot.

Buehrle rattled off 14 straight seasons of at least 200 innings pitched, and while he was never overpowering, he was the definition of a crafty left-hander who made the most of his stuff to win 214 games with a 3.81 ERA in 3,283.1 innings. He threw a no-hitter and a perfect game, and he won a World Series ring in 2005. He received 20.0 percent of the vote last year in his sixth year of eligibility.

Stats: 422 GS, 163-122, 3.43 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 2,560 K, 2,698.0 IP WAR: 59.0 Accolades: 4x All-Star, 1x WS winner

Cole Hamels won NLCS and World Series MVP as a 24-year-old in 2008 while leading the Phillies to a title, then settled in as a consistent frontline performer over 15 seasons in the majors.

He received Cy Young votes four times and made at least 30 starts in 10 different seasons as a durable, reliable rotation anchor, making good as a homegrown ace in Philadelphia.

The left-hander received a healthy 23.8 percent voting support in his first year on the ballot, which eclipsed the 20.6 percent that Félix Hernández received in his inaugural year of eligibility in 2025 before that spiked to 46.1 percent in year two.

Stats: 2,275 G, 95 OPS+, 2,455 H, 231 HR, 936 RBI, 470 SB WAR: 47.9 Accolades: 3x All-Star, 4x Gold Glove, 1x Silver Slugger, 1x NL MVP, 1x WS winner

Jimmy Rollins falls in the same "Hall of Very Good" range as guys like Bert Campaneris (53.1 WAR), Jim Fregosi (48.7 WAR), Miguel Tejada (47.1 WAR), Tony Fernandez (45.3 WAR) and Troy Tulowitzki (44.5 WAR) in terms of career WAR among shortstops.

His 2007 NL MVP award does raise his profile a bit higher, and he has a case for being the top shortstop of the era immediately following the primes of Derek Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Nomar Garciaparra and others.

His voting support has steadily improved in his five years on the ballot, from 9.4 to 12.9 to 14.8 to 18.0 to 25.4 percent, but he still has a long way to go.

Stats: 1,512 G, 113 OPS+, 1,805 H, 140 HR, 725 RBI, 138 SB

Accolades: 4x All-Star, 4x Gold Glove, 1x Silver Slugger, 1x AL MVP, 2x WS winner

The 2007 AL Rookie of the Year winner and 2008 AL MVP, Dustin Pedroia was a bona fide superstar for the Boston Red Sox who helped lead the team to World Series titles in 2007 and 2013.

A knee injury he suffered in his age-33 season cut his career short; otherwise, he might have ended up with a more compelling Hall of Fame case, though his peak stacks up to some of the all-time greats at the position.

His support jumped from 11.9 to 20.7 percent in 2026 in his second year of eligibility, and it will be interesting to see how Chase Utley's candidacy impacts his down the line.

Stats: 451 GS, 200-117, 3.66 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 2,488 K, 2,740.0 IP

One of the best postseason pitchers of his generation, Jon Lester logged a 2.51 ERA over 154 career playoff innings. That includes a 1.77 ERA and 0.93 WHIP over 35.2 innings in the World Series, where he went 4-1 across five starts and one relief appearance.

His signing signaled the end of the Cubs' rebuilding era and ushered in the contention window that resulted in a long-awaited World Series title in 2016, and he took home NLCS MVP honors during that playoff run.

His 2,488 strikeouts rank 41st on the all-time list and 13th among lefties, but it's his big-game reputation that will be the foundation of his Hall of Fame case.

Stats: 418 GS, 169-136, 3.42 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 2,524 K, 2,729.2 IP WAR: 49.8 Accolades: 6x All-Star, 1x Cy Young

Felix Hernández was squarely in the conversation for best pitcher in baseball at the peak of his career, which included 2010 AL Cy Young honors and three other top-five finishes in the balloting.

He made his MLB debut as a 19-year-old phenom, then promptly rattled off 10 straight seasons of at least 30 starts while anchoring the Seattle rotation. His 49.8 WAR is the fourth-highest mark in Mariners franchise history, well ahead of Randy Johnson (39.0) and behind only Ken Griffey Jr. (70.6), Edgar Martínez (68.4) and Ichiro Suzuki (56.4).

After a solid 20.6 percent showing in his first year on the ballot in 2025, he jumped up to 46.1 percent last year, putting him on a legitimate Cooperstown trajectory.

Stats: 521 GS, 256-153, 3.85 ERA, 1.35 WHIP, 2,448 K, 3,316.0 IP

It would be interesting to see what type of support Andy Pettitte would receive from voters if not for his admitted HGH use , which he said was intended to speed his recovery from an elbow injury.

With 256 wins and a 3.85 ERA over 3,316 innings, he does not have a slam-dunk case from a regular-season standpoint, but his 3.81 ERA over 276.2 innings in the playoffs and five World Series rings might have been enough to push him over the top.

After failing to reach 20 percent voting support in each of his first six years on the ballot, he jumped to 27.9 percent in 2025 and 48.5 percent in 2026, paving the way for a serious push in his final two years of eligibility.

Stats: 2,425 G, 128 OPS+, 2,470 H, 288 HR, 1,363 RBI, 400 SB WAR: 60.2 Accolades: 2x All-Star, 1x Gold Glove, 1x Silver Slugger

One of the most underrated players in MLB history, Bobby Abreu was an on-base machine throughout his career and a perennial 20/20 player during his prime with the Philadelphia Phillies.

He was a 5-WAR player seven different times over his 18-year career, and he ranks in the top 25 of all time in doubles (574, 25th) and walks (1,476, 20th).

Like several other players on a cleared out ballot last year, he reached new levels of support, garnering 30.8 percent of the vote after failing to reach the 20 percent threshold during his first six years of eligibility.

Stats: 2,784 G, 140 OPS+, 3,115 H, 696 HR, 2,086 RBI, 329 SB

Accolades: 14x All-Star, 2x Gold Glove, 10x Silver Slugger, 3x AL MVP, 1x WS winner

Alex Rodriguez serves as the unofficial dividing line between candidates with a realistic shot at election in 2027 and those facing longer odds, whether because they are still building support, have documented PED histories or fall into the "Hall of Very Good."

In terms of sheer statistical production, A-Rod is one of the greatest to ever play the game. He successfully lived up to the immense hype that surrounded him when he was chosen No. 1 overall in the 1993 draft and made his MLB debut a year later at the age of 18, quickly emerging as a superstar in Seattle.

Rodriguez admitted to using PEDs during his time with the Texas Rangers. After Barry Bonds exhausted his BBWAA ballot eligibility without reaching the 75 percent threshold, Rodriguez appears likely to suffer a similar fate.

So far, he has received 34.3, 35.7, 34.8, 37.1 and 40.0 percent of the vote in his five years on the ballot, gaining just 2.9 percentage points in 2026.

Stats: 1,371 G, 129 OPS+, 1,500 H, 158 HR, 729 RBI, 23 SB WAR: 45.0 Accolades: 7x All-Star, 5x Silver Slugger, 1x Gold Glove, 1x NL MVP, 3x WS winner

While he played just 12 seasons and does not have the counting numbers of the standard Hall of Famer as a result, Buster Posey still stands as one of the greatest catchers in MLB history.

He was at the center of the Giants winning three World Series titles in five years, with the first coming when he was the 2010 NL Rookie of the Year and the second when he was the 2012 NL MVP.

He is one of only five catchers to win a batting title, and he was a career .302/.372/.460 hitter. Joe Mauer getting in as a first-ballot selection in 2024 would seem to indicate he has a good chance of making a quick entrance into Cooperstown.

Stats: 1,937 G, 117 OPS+, 1,885 H, 259 HR, 1,025 RBI, 154 SB WAR: 64.5 Accolades: 6x All-Star, 4x Silver Slugger, 1x WS winner

During his first five seasons as an everyday player, Chase Utley hit .301/.388/.535 for a 135 OPS+ while averaging 39 doubles, 29 home runs, 101 RBI, 111 runs scored and 7.9 WAR.

A few more seasons of that peak performance would have given him a more compelling body of work, but he was already 26 years old when he finally earned an everyday role. Still, his 64.5 WAR ranks 15th all-time among second basemen, slotted right in between Hall of Famers Craig Biggio (65.5) and Jackie Robinson (63.9).

For comparison's sake, Biggio received 68.2 percent of the vote in his first year on the ballot and took three years to get over the hump. Utley has gone from 28.8 to 39.8 to 59.1 percent in his first three years of eligibility, so things are trending toward a possible 2027 induction.

articles.title: Predicting How MLB's Free-Agent Pitching Market Shakes Out
articles.summary: Even if the consensus on this winter's MLB free-agent market is that it consists of a weak crop of players, it's also lopsided in a way that offers a silver lining.
articles.body:
Even if the consensus on this winter's MLB free-agent market is that it consists of a weak crop of players, it's also lopsided in a way that offers a silver lining.

The bats may not be good, but there's no shortage of quality arms. Tarik Skubal is positioned to become the most expensive free-agent pitcher in history. There are a handful of other starting pitchers who could crack nine figures, and there might even be a reliever who gets up into that range.

With the lockout looming and early deals for Emilio Pagán and Evan Phillips having gotten the market moving, there's no time like the present to guess where the other top available arms will end up.

Ahead are predictions for nine pitchers: two relievers, six starters and one Japanese phenom who is looking to come to MLB straight out of high school.

With Emilio Pagán and Evan Phillips off the board, David Bednar is a solid pick to be the next big domino to fall on the market for relievers.

How Phillips' market, in particular, panned out should bode well for Bednar. MLB Trade Rumors had projected the longtime Los Angeles Dodgers righty for a two-year, $24 million contract. He actually got three years, $35 million from the Atlanta Braves, which ups the bar for leverage relievers of all stripes.

Assuming the next CBA doesn't nix the current system, the catch with Bednar is that he'll be tied to draft pick compensation if he rejects a $23.15 million qualifying offer from the New York Yankees. He hasn't officially done so yet, which could explain a lack of hard rumors on who's poking around his neck of the woods.

The Yankees are obviously the incumbent in this race, and most predictions have them finding a way to keep Bednar in their pen.

As per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com, Yankees GM Brian Cashman has referred to the bullpen as "our main priority." He's already acted on that by bringing back lefty Tim Hill on a one-year, $2.25 million deal. That leaves plenty of room in their offseason budget for more signings, including a contract for Bednar that would pay out eight figures per year.

They also have an advantage over other teams that would enter the race for the two-time All-Star closer: Whereas other teams would face penalties for signing him if he rejects the qualifying offer, the Yankees won't.

Adrian Morejon began the winter as the best reliever on the free agent market, and he soon cleared something up: He does, in fact, want to remain a reliever .

Though the 27-year-old probably could be a good starter, even his All-Star credentials as a reliever might undersell how good he is at the job. Per Pitching+ , he was the best overall bullpen arm in MLB this year.

That plus his age could make teams more forgiving of his ties to the qualifying offer, which he's sure to reject. Popular speculative landing spots include the Yankees, Chicago Cubs and Los Angeles Dodgers, though Kevin Barral of Fish on First also puts the Miami Marlins in the race.

Given their prior reluctance to go hard after free agents under Jerry Dipoto, the Mariners might actually be a long-shot pick for Morejon.

However, Ryan Divish of The Seattle Times has reported that A) the Mariners are indeed interested and B) that their 2027 payroll is going to be in the $175-180 million range , which equates to at least $30 million in flexibility for new salaries.

Dipoto has otherwise been open about wanting leverage relievers , and going in that direction might be his best hope of a free agent splash. As much as he also needs bats, T-Mobile Park might as well have a "Keep Out" sign hanging on it.

After a dazzling high school career, Shoki Oda was projected to be a first-round pick in October's NPB draft. Instead, he decided to pursue opportunities in the United States , either by signing with an MLB organization or attending an American college.

There should perhaps be quotation marks around "MLB career," given the 18-year-old will be signed as an international amateur who will then have to work his way through the minors. He's not the next coming of Roki Sasaki. At least, not yet.

Whatever the case, Francys Romero has the New York Mets, Philadelphia Phillies, St. Louis Cardinals, Toronto Blue Jays and Houston Astros in the hunt for Oda. He's also known to have met with the Yankees ( Brendan Kuty of The Athletic) and Dodgers ( Dylan Hernandez of the New York Post ).

Per Kuty, the Yankees' meeting with Oda included billionaire minority owner Soichiro Minami along with a handful of front office types. They're clearly taking their pursuit seriously.

The Dodgers, though, have had the longest meeting (over three hours, per Hernandez) with Oda so far. They have also touted him as the best 18-year-old pitcher in the world, and the most talented arm to come out of Japan since Sasaki.

So, they're also serious. It's also hard to count them out whenever they like a present or future star from Japan, and the corner Sasaki turned for them this year should help convince Oda that he'd be in good hands with them.

Whereas Shoki Oda is a long-term project for MLB teams, Kaima Taira offers multiple potential pathways to immediate success.

He's coming to MLB fresh off a stellar turn (1.36 ERA, 0.959 WHIP) as a starter for the Seibu Lions, with an arsenal consisting of a high-90s fastball and a diverse array of secondaries. As recently as 2024 and 2025, though, it was as a dominant reliever that Taira was a star in Japan.

According to Bruce Levine of 670 The Score, both Chicago clubs are in on Taira's market. Kevin Acee of the San Diego Union-Tribune has the Padres in the mix as well. Taira is also a fit for any number of starter-needy teams, such as the Mets, Blue Jays, Astros and Orioles.

White Sox GM Chris Getz made no bones about his search for starting pitching during the GM Meetings, telling James Fegan of the Chicago Sun-Times : "It's our top priority. We feel pretty good about the depth, but we do want to find ways to upgrade the quality of the innings in the rotation."

With Taira, it may not hurt Getz's cause that he can tout a recent success story with a Japanese star. Getz believed in Munetaka Murakami when most clearly did not last winter, and that worked out wonderfully for the South Siders.

Given the uncertainty over his best role in MLB, the White Sox's willingness to be flexible with how they use pitchers could work to Taira's advantage. They had 13 pitchers both open and close a game this year.

Among the tried-and-true MLB starters on the market, Sonny Gray represents the demarcation line between mid-level arms like Kevin Gausman, Casey Mize, Clay Holmes and Dustin May and the top of the class.

Because he's 37 years old, he's likely looking at a one- or two-year deal. With the Boston Red Sox having declined their side of his $30 million mutual option, that figure provides a benchmark for his next total guarantee.

Per Alex Speier of the Boston Globe , Gray is open to returning to the Red Sox following a 2026 season that saw him finish fifth in the AL Cy Young Award voting. Also according to Speier , however, it's seen as unlikely.

There have yet to be solid rumors on which way Gray's market is trending, but the Braves just keep coming up as a speculative landing spot.

It's an "obvious fit," in the words of Will Sammon and Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic, and they're not wrong. The Braves need another top-of-the-rotation arm to pair with Chris Sale, and they have geography in their favor. Gray lives in Nashville and is said to prefer to pitch close to home.

Even after signing Evan Phillips, the Braves still have about $30 million in spending capacity before their 2027 payroll matches their 2026 payroll. That's enough for Gray.

Freddy Peralta was headed toward "reclamation project" status as a free agent when he was with the Mets, but getting traded to the Tampa Bay Rays changed everything.

Just for starters, it rendered him ineligible for a qualifying offer. He then found his All-Star form again during Tampa Bay's run to the World Series, winning ALCS MVP and ultimately pitching to a 1.82 ERA between September and October.

The Padres are interested in Peralta, according to ESPN's Alden Gonzalez . He's also a speculative fit for clubs like the Blue Jays, Orioles, White Sox and Cubs, the latter of whom were called an "obvious fit" by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic.

Obvious fit, indeed. From his eight years with the Milwaukee Brewers, Peralta has ample experience in the NL Central. More to the point, he has a connection to Cubs manager Craig Counsell, who managed Milwaukee from 2015 to 2023.

There's also the elephant in the room that concerns who the Cubs aren't chasing in free agency. As much as they clearly need a pitcher of his caliber in their rotation, Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic reported that the Cubs "appear unlikely" to pursue Tarik Skubal.

That reluctance is hard to justify for a team with such a strong revenue stream, but it's unfortunately typical of what Cubs fans have come to expect. Peralta's likely asking price and lack of draft-pick compensation requirements make him a better match for the club's risk aversion.

It was only last winter that Michael King signed a three-year, $75 million contract to stay with the Padres, but he rightfully opted out of that after posting a 3.21 ERA across 185.0 innings this season.

The 31-year-old righty did leave $58 million on the table, but he has more than just the helium of his 2026 campaign working in his favor. After getting one last year, he was ineligible for a qualifying offer this time around.

The Blue Jays are engaged with King, according to Ben Nicholson-Smith of Sportsnet.ca. He's otherwise a possibility for the Mets, Cubs and White Sox, the latter of whom recently got a vote of confidence from Bob Nightengale of USA Today.

There's also the possibility of a return to the Padres, which makes sense simply based on their obvious need to build up their rotation this winter.

They could go all-in on a pursuit of Tarik Skubal, which would allow José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones to make a strong impression in their first offseason as the team's owners. There's only so much money to go around, however, and he'd be just one addition for a rotation that needs several.

Besides, why mess with a good thing? Whereas King has ample bust potential elsewhere, he and the Padres know they can work well together.

Trevor Rogers is to the 2026-27 market what Zack Wheeler was to the 2019-20 market once upon a time: A chance to get in on the ground level with a starter who has not yet peaked as an ace.

He was an All-Star and a Rookie of the Year contender in 2021, plus a down-ballot candidate for the AL Cy Young Award in 2025. He only has a career 107 ERA+ despite all this, yet the stuff and command to do better are there. Just as important, he just turned 29 on November 13.

Usual suspects like the Mets, Padres and White Sox are candidates to sign Rogers. The Cubs are also interested in the left-hander, according to Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic.

Since the Blue Jays have yet to be firmly connected to Rogers, this is going out on a bit of a limb.

What we do know, however, is that they need starting pitching and have been poking around the top pitchers on the market. As noted earlier, that includes Michael King. It also includes Tarik Skubal, according to Mitch Bannon and Will Sammon of The Athletic .

Rogers represents an obvious pivot if the Blue Jays can't land either of them, especially given that he has plenty of experience with their AL East foes.

Tarik Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner with a 2.42 ERA and 0.923 WHIP to show for his last three seasons. His creds don't need more elaboration than that.

According to Ronald Blum of the Associated Press, Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, have meetings with six teams lined up. Those include the Mets, Dodgers, Padres and Blue Jays, plus two mystery teams. If the Cubs are not among those mystery teams, those first four clubs might represent Skubal's top landing spots.

One thing, though: Per Jeff Passan of ESPN, Skubal and Boras have "no interest in a shorter-term, higher-dollar deal." It'll take a long-term contract to ride this ride.

If Skubal and Boras are indeed out on shorter deals, that could disadvantage the Dodgers. Such deals are their specialty, and Katie Woo of The Athletic had recently floated them applying the concept to retain Skubal.

If the Dodgers don't push their comfort zone, it could be Mets or bust for Skubal. It's a good thing for him, then, that they badly need a No. 1 starter and that Steve Cohen has historically shown a willingness to throw caution to the wind in free agency.

If Skubal is going to get the record contract that he's widely projected to get, expect it to land him in Queens.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Ketel Marte Trade Would Be Key to Orioles Boosting Playoff Chances Amid MLB Rumors
articles.summary: The continued inability of the Baltimore Orioles to put together a winning season, with a legitimate shot at competing for the World Series, resulted in the trade of Adley Rutschman to the Boston Red Sox in 2026, and what should be other significant changes to the roster this offseason.
articles.body:
The continued inability of the Baltimore Orioles to put together a winning season, with a legitimate shot at competing for the World Series, resulted in the trade of Adley Rutschman to the Boston Red Sox in 2026, and what should be other significant changes to the roster this offseason.

Orioles beat writer Jake Rill reported that the team has had communication with the Arizona Diamondbacks regarding second baseman Ketel Marte.

Any potential trade has to be approved by Marte himself, thanks to a no-trade clause, but the Orioles should do everything in their power to acquire the veteran player.

For the last five seasons, the front office has leaned on its core of young players, pointing to the likes of Rutschman, shortstop Gunnar Henderson, outfielders Colton Cowser and Jordan Westburg, and second baseman Jackson Holliday as the future of the club's success.

The decision to trade Rutschman hurt the fans' trust in general manager Mike Elias. The young core's underperformance created questions about their ability to win.

In fact, it was the team's prized free-agent signing, Pete Alonso, who encouraged excitement, thanks to his 43 home runs, 113 RBI, and .267/.363/.522 slash line.

His success proved to the fans that they do not have to wait for a young prospect to develop or for Henderson to rediscover his swing at the plate. They do not need to hope that Westburg and Cowser stay healthy, or that Holliday finds the talent that made him the most coveted young player in the game.

They can find winners in free agency, which has been the antithesis of what Elias and his front office team have done in recent years.

Marte is a talented hitter who gets on base and drives in runs. While 2026 was a down season for him, he still averaged .249, delivered 22 home runs, and 76 RBI. He has plenty to offer the Orioles at the plate and defensively.

As long as he is committed and wants to play in Baltimore, and does not disappear and no-show games , as was the case this past August, he is a great fit for a hungry organization.

He would also bring added veteran presence to the clubhouse, something the Orioles need. That he has been to a World Series, the place the team and its fans so badly want to get, is only further reason for the front office to reach a deal with the Diamondbacks.

Even if it means having to give up one or two of those young prospects to make it happen.

articles.title: Latest 2026 MLB Free Agents Rumors, Predictions on Tarik Skubal, Teruaki Sato and More
articles.summary: The free agency period in MLB figures to be one of the hottest, most unpredictable in baseball, with all eyes on ace Tarik Skubal and the looming lockout.
articles.body:
The free agency period in MLB figures to be one of the hottest, most unpredictable in baseball, with all eyes on ace Tarik Skubal and the looming lockout.

What is the latest on the two-time Cy Young Award winner and who else is garnering attention?

Find out in this collection from the game's top insiders.

Padres Targeting Skubal, Starting Pitching

The San Diego Padres fell short, again, in their pursuit of a World Series and reportedly have their eye on starting pitching in free agency.

ESPN's Alden Gonzalez reported, "In their quest to fill a variety of spots in their rotation, the Padres have set up a meeting with Tarik Skubal but have also expressed interest in Freddy Peralta, among other free agent starters, and are open to reunions with Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Nick Martinez."

Skubal is the belle of the ball in this year's free agency class and has garnered attention from the rival Los Angeles Dodgers and the New York Mets. Whether the Padres will be willing to outbid them remains to be seen.

Peralta was the ALCS MVP following a stellar performance on the mound, but was beaten up in the World Series, where he accumulated a 9.64 ERA in one start.

Still, he did more than enough from August on, after a trade sent him from the Mets to the Rays, to earn considerable attention (and a big payday) this offseason.

Reunions with King, Pivetta, and Martinez would be welcome, but Padres fans are going to demand something fresh and new after the team fell in the NLDS to the eventual World Series Champion Padres.

Peralta would be a great start for the Padres front office, at the right price, of course.

Prediction: Padres get a new starter, but miss out on Skubal

Unlike the Padres, the Orioles are not in the hunt to acquire Skubal, according to ESPN's Jorge Castillo .

"Baltimore is also looking to address the starting rotation, with Trevor Rogers hitting free agency. The Orioles won't be vying for Skubal's or the free agent pitchers in the tier below that, but they're poised to add a midrotation hurler," he wrote.

That should be of no surprise to anyone who has paid attention to, or followed, general manager Mike Elias' stint with the Orioles.

The team has never spent on a free agent ace, instead utilizing trades to acquire Corbin Burnes from Milwaukee and Zach Eflin from Tampa Bay in 2024.

Since then, the team has put together rotations via patchwork, leaning on prospects and veteran arms. It has not worked often, with the Orioles repeatedly producing teams that struggled on the mound.

Rogers was mostly a positive addition, with a year of dominance in 2025 and a so-so season adversely affected by injury in 2026. It remains to be seen if this is year that Elias strikes gold and the Orioles' rotation improves exponentially.

Prediction: The Orioles add a veteran arm, such as David Peterson, Nick Martinez, or Tyler Mahle.

Phillies Interested in Pair of Japanese Players

The Philadelphia Phillies faded during the playoffs, losing two-of-three to the Atlanta Braves and raising questions about the future of the roster.

Alec Bohm, Luis Arreaz, Edmundo Sosa, and Bryan De La Cruz are all free agents and the team will be looking to upgrade its bats this offseason.

Castillo reported, "Philadelphia has expressed strong interest in Japanese stars Seiya Suzuki and Teruaki Sato."

Suzuki is one of the game's best hitters and in 2026, averaging .270, with 26 homers, 86 RBI, and 147 total hits. He would be an instant upgrade for the Phillies, both as a designated hitter and outfielder.

Sato is a potential offensive dynamo who is posted by the Hanshin Tigers and available to sign before the December 1 collective bargaining agreement ends. He averaged .306, hit 39 home runs, and had a career-high OPS of .991 in 2026.

He figures to be one of the most intriguing potential adds this offseason.

Either would theoretically improve the Phillies offensively, but Suzuki is a proven commodity and would solve two of the team's issues at once.

articles.title: Alex Rodriguez, Buster Posey, Cole Hamels Headline 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame Ballot
articles.summary: The 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame ballot was officially unveiled on Monday.
articles.body:
The 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame ballot was officially unveiled on Monday.

In his sixth year of eligibility, Alex Rodriguez headlines a list of 13 returnees from the 2026 ballot, along with Cole Hamels. Three-time World Series champion Buster Posey leads the way among 14 newcomers. The full list of candidates is as follows:

MLB announced that the voting results will be revealed on Jan. 19 on MLB Network at 6 p.m. ET. Players who receive at least 75 percent of the vote from the BBWAA will be inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, N.Y., on July 25. This year's three-person class of inductees included Carlos Beltran, Andruw Jones and Jeff Kent.

Rodriguez received 40 percent of the vote on the 2026 ballot, up from 37.1 percent in 2025. Despite being a three-time American League MVP and a World Series champion who ranks fifth in MLB history with 696 home runs, the 51-year-old's admission of using performance-enhancing drugs during his career has surely impacted his Hall of Fame candidacy.

Hamels had the highest voting percentage of any player who debuted on the 2026 ballot at 23.8 percent. The four-time All-Star was one of the most dominant starting pitchers of his generation, throwing 2,560 strikeouts.

Posey, who now serves as the president of baseball operations for the San Francisco Giants, is widely regarded as one of the greatest catchers of all time. He won the National League batting title and MVP award in 2012, capping off that season with the second of his three career World Series titles.

All BBWAA ballots must be submitted by Dec. 31, and we will learn the inductees in the 2027 Hall of Fame class early next year.

articles.title: MLB reveals 2027 Hall of Fame ballot with 14 first-timers and 13 returnees
articles.summary: This year's ballot is led by Chase Utley and Alex Rodriguez, with newcomers Buster Posey and Jon Lester also included.
articles.body:
MLB is in the offseason, and a lockout looms.

While Collective Bargaining Agreement discussions could derail next season's start, they do not affect the voting process for the next Baseball Hall of Fame class.

On Monday, MLB revealed the 27 players on the 2027 Hall of Fame ballot .

Baseball Hall of Fame voting comes down to the Baseball Writers' Association of America (BBWAA). Writers are eligible if they have been active baseball writers for 10 years. For last year's class, 425 BBWAA voting members participated.

Each writer may vote for a maximum of 10 players on their ballot. Some writers choose to vote for 10 players; others turn in blank ballots.

Players are eligible as long as they have had at least a 10-year career and have been retired for at least 5 years. A BBWAA committee of six members nominates possible first-time candidates, and they make the ballot if at least two committee members nominate them.

To be elected to MLB's Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, players must receive a vote on at least 75% of ballots.

Do players automatically stay on the ballot for next year?

No. A player must receive a vote on at least 5% of ballots cast to remain on the ballot for the following year.

How long can players remain on the ballot?

Players are automatically removed from the ballot after 10 years, provided that they received a vote on at least 5% of ballots every year to remain on the ballot for 10 years.

Is anyone in their final year of eligibility in 2027?

Omar Vizquel. This is his 10th year on the ballot, and he received a vote on 18.4% of ballots last year, so he would be considered quite the long shot to make it.

Who has the best chance to make it this year?

It is hard to predict exactly how the BBWAA voting will go. Alex Rodriguez is on the ballot for the sixth time and is the most high-profile "steroid era" player still eligible. He got a vote on 40% of ballots last year.

Second baseman Chase Utley jumped to 59.1% of ballots last year and is now in his fourth year on the ballot. He is the only returnee who was on at least 50% of ballots last year.

For newcomers, San Francisco Giants catcher Buster Posey has the best chance to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer. He was the 2010 NL Rookie of the Year, 2012 NL MVP, and won three World Series titles with San Francisco in five years. Posey played in just 12 seasons, but was a seven-time All-Star, five-time Silver Slugger and had a career WAR of 45.

Jon Lester could be a name to watch given his postseason track record, but even that likely won't be enough to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer.
